analysis.one_liner: Gives student loan borrowers clear statements, error fixes, and the right to sue loan servicers and private lenders.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first committee referral and died without a vote in the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required companies that handle student loans to tell borrowers what they owe, answer their questions, offer help before default, and stop hiding behind forced arbitration clauses that block borrowers from suing. It covered both private student loans and federal loans handled by private servicing companies. It was introduced in May 2019 and referred to the Senate's education committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: People repaying student loans — including federal borrowers whose loans are handled by private servicing companies, private loan borrowers, active-duty service members, and veterans — would get clearer billing, faster answers on errors, targeted help before default, and access to the courts.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers, including service members

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders and servicers to send detailed monthly statements showing rates, balances, fees, and how payments were applied, and to disclose alternative repayment options before the first fully amortized payment is due [S2] [S3].

Requires servicers to designate trained repayment specialists for borrowers at risk of default, to respond to written borrower inquiries within set deadlines, and to fix payment allocation so excess payments go to the highest-interest loan first [S2] [S3].
Bans mandatory arbitration clauses and class action waivers in student loan agreements, restoring borrowers' right to sue servicers in court [S2] [S3].
Gives servicemembers and veterans a dedicated liaison at each servicer and prohibits charging off or reporting loans of active-duty borrowers in combat zones [S2] [S3].

Cancels private student loans on death or total permanent disability, limits late fees, and lets borrowers rehabilitate a defaulted private loan and have the charge-off removed from their credit history [S2] [S3].

Requires colleges to certify private loans and tell students about federal aid options first, and requires lenders to warn borrowers what federal benefits they give up when refinancing federal loans into private ones [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Student loan servicers and private student lenders would bear the cost of new disclosure, staffing, and complaint-handling requirements, would lose late-fee and convenience-fee revenue, and would lose the arbitration clauses that currently shield them from class action lawsuits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Loan servicers and private student lenders

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on servicing companies, which could translate into slower service, layoffs in the servicing industry, or pressure to raise other charges; servicers have long argued federal contract rules already constrain what they can change on federal loans [S3].

The bill adds extensive new reporting and rulemaking duties for the Education Department and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, including a new interagency working group, which means significant regulatory implementation work [S2] [S3].
Eliminating arbitration and class action waivers increases litigation risk for lenders, a cost that critics argue can be passed on to future borrowers through higher rates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address well-documented borrower complaints — opaque statements, payment misallocation, unhelpful servicers, and no recourse in court — and the main costs are compliance expenses for servicing companies and possible pass-through pricing. The bill does not forgive debt or lower interest rates, so it helps borrowers mainly by making repayment fairer and more transparent rather than cheaper.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Student Loan Borrower Bill of Rights on May 7, 2019, with Sen. Reed and Sen. Warren as original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded — and the bill expired at the end of the 116th Congress [S5] [S1].
The bill attracted 9 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support listed [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan servicers and private lenders are better off because the bill died: they keep the current disclosure rules, fee practices, and arbitration clauses the bill would have restricted. Borrowers who needed help avoiding default or suing servicers gained nothing from the bill's failure, but paid nothing either — the protections were never enacted anywhere else in this Congress through this bill.

for.role: U.S. Senators from Rhode Island and Massachusetts

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor was listed.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to expire.

against.name: Student loan servicing industry
against.role: Federal loan servicers and private student lenders
against.what_they_did: The bill's disclosure, fee, arbitration, and litigation provisions targeted this industry's practices; it was the interest the bill was written against, and it benefited from the bill never advancing.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and the Senate committee majority that let the bill sit was Republican; no Republican support is recorded anywhere in the bill's history.

industries.note: Servicers would face detailed disclosure duties, mandatory repayment specialists, response deadlines, fee limits, and an end to class action waivers — all aimed at practices borrowers have complained about for years. The industry's gain from the bill dying is keeping the status quo.

Lenders would lose mandatory arbitration and class action waivers, face death and disability discharge requirements, and need school certification of each loan, but the credit-reporting rehabilitation program would let them recover some defaulted borrowers. Their core interest in the bill was blocking the restrictions, since restrictions cut into collection tactics.

Charge-offs and collections would face new limits, including a ban on charging off combat-zone service members' loans, but the rehabilitation pathway would move some defaulted loans back into good standing and back into collection pipelines.
